REIGNITE / INNER TRADITIONS / GNOSTICISM

Christian Gnosticism

γνῶσις · gnōsis · “knowing”

A family of early Christian movements holding that salvation comes through direct experiential knowledge of the divine — not through belief, institutional membership, or assent to doctrine.

What It Is

The word gnosis is Greek for knowledge, but not the kind you get from being told something. It means knowledge by acquaintance — the difference between reading about a city and having walked its streets. Gnostic teachers held that the decisive knowledge concerned the self: that a spark of the divine is present within each person, that it originates outside the material order, and that recognising it is what liberation consists of.

For most of history these movements were known almost entirely through the writings of their opponents — heresiologists like Irenaeus, who described Gnostic teaching in order to refute it. That changed in December 1945, when a farmer near Nag Hammadi in Upper Egypt unearthed a sealed jar containing thirteen leather-bound papyrus codices. They held fifty-two texts in Coptic, most previously unknown, dating to roughly the fourth century and translated from earlier Greek originals. For the first time these traditions could be read in their own voice.

The tradition is not monolithic. Valentinus taught in Rome in the second century and was, by some accounts, nearly elected bishop; his school produced sophisticated theological writing. Basilides taught in Alexandria. The Sethian and Thomasine currents differ from both. What they share is an emphasis on interior transformation and a suspicion that the visible religious order is not the whole story.

The figure of Sophia — Wisdom — sits at the centre of the Gnostic cosmological myth: a divine emanation whose descent into the material world sets the human situation in motion, and whose restoration is bound up with its resolution.

Core Teachings

  • GnosisDirect, experiential knowledge of the divine — distinguished sharply from pistis (belief) and from doctrinal assent. It is described as a recognition rather than an acquisition.
  • The Divine SparkA fragment of the transcendent source held to be present within each person, obscured by material existence and by forgetting. Awakening it is the aim.
  • PleromaThe fullness — the realm of divine emanation from which the spark originates and to which it returns. Often depicted as a series of paired emanations (aeons) proceeding from an unknowable source.
  • The DemiurgeThe craftsman who fashions the material world while mistakenly believing himself to be the highest God — a figure of ignorance rather than straightforward evil in most Gnostic texts.
  • SophiaWisdom, personified as a divine emanation whose descent precipitates the material order. Her name is the root of the word philosophy — love of wisdom.
  • Self-Knowledge“Know thyself” functions here as a theological instruction rather than a proverb: to know oneself truly is held to be inseparable from knowing the source.

Practice & Method

  • Contemplative ReadingThe sayings texts — above all the Gospel of Thomas — are structured as objects for sustained meditation rather than narrative. Thomas opens by telling the reader that whoever finds the interpretation of these sayings will not taste death, framing the whole text as a practice.
  • Interior InquirySustained self-examination aimed at distinguishing the conditioned self from what the texts call the living one within — closer to contemplative introspection than to moral self-audit.
  • Initiation & SacramentValentinian communities practised sacramental rites including baptism, anointing and what the Gospel of Philip calls the bridal chamber — read by most scholars as symbolic of the reunion of the divided self.
  • Teacher TransmissionInstruction passed between teacher and student rather than through institutional office, which is part of why the tradition left little organisational trace and was easily displaced.

Learn More — Primary Texts & Reputable Sources

  • The Nag Hammadi LibraryFull English translations of all fifty-two texts, with scholarly introductions — the primary corpus, free to read.gnosis.org
  • Claremont Colleges Digital Library — Nag Hammadi ArchivePhotographic archive of the original codices and excavation records, from the institution that led their study.ccdl.claremont.edu
  • Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy — GnosticismPeer-reviewed scholarly overview of the philosophical content and the historiographical debates around the category itself.plato.stanford.edu
  • Britannica — GnosticismConcise, edited reference introduction with historical context.britannica.com
  • Elaine Pagels — The Gnostic GospelsThe standard popular introduction, by the Princeton historian whose work brought Nag Hammadi to a general readership. National Book Award, 1980.Princeton University
REIGNITE / INNER TRADITIONS / SUFISM

Sufism

تصوّف · taṣawwuf

The inner dimension of Islam: the purification of the heart and the disciplined path toward direct knowledge of God — practised within the tradition, not alongside it.

What It Is

Sufism is best understood not as a sect but as the interior science of Islam. Its foundational reference is the hadith of Gabriel, in which the angel questions the Prophet on three levels of the religion: islām (outward practice), īmān (belief), and iḥsān — defined as worshipping God as though you see Him, and knowing that if you do not see Him, He sees you. Taṣawwuf is the cultivation of that third level.

The Arabic name is taṣawwuf. The English word “Sufi” likely derives from ṣūf, the coarse wool worn by early ascetics in Basra and Kufa. From the eighth century onward the tradition developed from individual ascetic practice into structured paths of instruction.

Its organisational form is the ṭarīqa — an order transmitting a specific method through an unbroken chain (silsila) of teachers. The major historical orders include the Qadiriyya, Naqshbandiyya, Chishtiyya, Shadhiliyya and Mevlevi, each with its own emphases and practices.

Sufism produced some of the most widely read literature in world history. Jalāl al-Dīn Rūmī, whose Masnavi runs to some 25,000 verses, remains among the most-read poets in the English language nearly eight centuries after his death. Abū Ḥāmid al-Ghazālī, one of the most influential theologians in Islamic history, abandoned a prestigious professorship in Baghdad for years of solitary practice and returned to argue that the inner path was indispensable to the religion — an argument that substantially secured Sufism's place within Sunni orthodoxy.

Core Teachings

  • IḥsānSpiritual excellence — to worship as though you see God. The aim of the entire path, defined in the hadith of Gabriel.
  • Tazkiyat al-NafsPurification of the lower self. The nafs is described in stages, from the self that commands to evil, through the self-reproaching soul, to the soul at peace — a developmental sequence with roots in the Qurān.
  • QalbThe heart, understood as the organ of spiritual perception rather than of sentiment. Polishing it until it can reflect reality is the central metaphor of the tradition.
  • Fanāʾ & BaqāʾAnnihilation of the ego-self in the divine, and subsistence afterward — the return to ordinary life transformed. The second is regarded as the higher and more difficult station.
  • Maqāmāt & AḥwālStations and states. Stations are earned through effort and retained; states are given, transient, and not under the seeker's control — a distinction that guards against spiritual pride.
  • TawḥīdThe divine unity. Realised in the Sufi reading not merely as a doctrine to be affirmed but as a truth to be directly known, ultimately dissolving the sense of a separate self standing apart from God.

Practice & Method

  • DhikrRemembrance — the rhythmic invocation of the divine names, alone or in assembly, silently or aloud. The central practice of nearly every order, grounded in the Qurānic instruction that hearts find rest in the remembrance of God.
  • MurāqabaWatchfulness — sustained meditative attention to the divine presence, and to the movements of one's own soul under that gaze.
  • Suḥba & SilsilaCompanionship with a qualified teacher, within a documented chain of transmission. The tradition holds the path is not safely walked from books alone.
  • SamāʿSpiritual audition — listening to recited poetry and music as a contemplative practice. The Mevlevi order's turning ceremony is its most widely known form, though samāʿ is debated and not practised by every order.
  • KhalwaRetreat — periods of structured seclusion for intensive practice, undertaken under a teacher's direction.

Learn More — Primary Texts & Reputable Sources

  • Oxford Bibliographies — SufismAnnotated scholarly bibliography of the field, maintained by specialists — the best starting map of the academic literature.oxfordbibliographies.com
  • Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy — Ibn ʿArabīPeer-reviewed treatment of the most systematically philosophical figure in the tradition.plato.stanford.edu
  • Britannica — SufismEdited reference overview of the history, orders and doctrines.britannica.com
  • Dar al-MasnaviScholarly translations and commentary on Rūmī's Masnavi by Ibrahim Gamard, working from the Persian rather than from popular English renderings.dar-al-masnavi.org
  • Al-Ghazālī — Deliverance from ErrorAl-Ghazālī's own account of his crisis of certainty and turn to the Sufi path — a primary source and one of the earliest spiritual autobiographies in any language.ghazali.org
REIGNITE / INNER TRADITIONS / KABBALAH

Kabbalah

קַבָּלָה · qabbalāh · “receiving”

The Jewish inner tradition: a body of teaching on the structure of divine emanation, the hidden dimension of Torah, and the human role in the repair of a fractured world.

What It Is

The name means receiving — which already says something about the tradition's self-understanding. Kabbalah presents itself not as speculation but as transmission: teaching handed down, received rather than invented.

Jewish mystical practice long predates the term. Merkavah mysticism, from roughly the first centuries CE, concerned ascent through the heavenly palaces toward the divine throne of Ezekiel's vision. Sefer Yetzirah, the Book of Formation, is an extremely terse early text on creation through the letters of the Hebrew alphabet and ten primordial numbers.

Kabbalah proper emerges in the twelfth and thirteenth centuries in Provence and Spain. Its central work is the Zohar — the Book of Radiance — a sprawling mystical commentary on the Torah written in Aramaic, presented as the teaching of the second-century sage Shimon bar Yochai, and attributed by modern scholarship to Moses de León in thirteenth-century Castile.

The tradition's decisive systematisation came in sixteenth-century Safed, in the Galilee, through Isaac Luria — known as the Ari. Luria wrote almost nothing; his teaching survives chiefly through his student Chaim Vital. Lurianic Kabbalah reframed the entire tradition around a cosmic drama of contraction, shattering and repair, and its vocabulary has shaped Jewish thought ever since. Hasidism, founded in the eighteenth century by the Baal Shem Tov, brought this inner world to ordinary communities as lived devotional practice.

Core Teachings

  • Ein SofThe Infinite — the divine as it is in itself, without limit and beyond all attribute, name or conception. Everything the tradition describes concerns not Ein Sof but its self-disclosure.
  • The SefirotTen emanations through which the infinite becomes manifest — Keter, Chochmah, Binah, Chesed, Gevurah, Tiferet, Netzach, Hod, Yesod, Malchut — arranged as the Etz Chaim, the Tree of Life, in three pillars balancing expansion, restraint and harmony.
  • TzimtzumContraction. Luria's central image: the infinite withdraws from a point in order to make room for a world to exist at all. Creation begins with an act of self-limitation rather than of assertion.
  • Shevirat ha-KelimThe shattering of the vessels — the vessels meant to hold the divine light break under it, scattering sparks throughout creation. The world as we find it is described as the aftermath of this rupture.
  • Tikkun OlamRepair of the world. Each act performed with proper intention is held to raise a scattered spark toward its source. This is where the tradition's cosmology becomes ethics — and the phrase has since entered general Jewish and secular usage far from its Lurianic origin.
  • DevekutCleaving — sustained attachment of the mind and heart to the divine, sought within ordinary life rather than apart from it. The practical aim of much Hasidic teaching.

Practice & Method

  • Talmud TorahStudy as contemplative practice. In this tradition study is not preparation for the spiritual life; it is the spiritual life, and the text is approached as having depths beyond its plain sense.
  • KavanotIntentions — specific contemplative focuses directed toward the sefirot during prayer, transforming fixed liturgy into an inner working. Lurianic kavanot are highly elaborate.
  • HitbodedutSecluded personal prayer — unstructured, spoken aloud in one's own words and language. Central to Breslov Hasidism, which recommends a set period daily.
  • Letter MeditationThe ecstatic method associated with Abraham Abulafia in thirteenth-century Spain: permutation and visualisation of Hebrew letters and divine names, combined with breath and posture, aimed at prophetic states.
  • Traditional RestrictionCustom has historically limited advanced study to mature students already grounded in Talmud and halakhah — often cited as age forty. The restriction is customary rather than legal, is debated, and is not observed uniformly, but it reflects a real caution about the material.

Learn More — Primary Texts & Reputable Sources

  • Sefaria — Kabbalah LibraryFree, searchable primary texts in Hebrew and Aramaic with English translation, including the Zohar and Sefer Yetzirah. The single best primary-source resource available.sefaria.org
  • Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy — Jewish MysticismPeer-reviewed scholarly overview of the philosophical dimensions and historical development.plato.stanford.edu
  • My Jewish Learning — Kabbalah & MysticismAccessible, well-edited introductions written by scholars for a general readership.myjewishlearning.com
  • Britannica — KabbalaEdited reference overview of the history and principal doctrines.britannica.com

Ron Hernandez
Software Engineer / Engineering Manager

I was born in El Salvador 🇸🇻 and moved to the United States 🇺🇸 at age 12. I attended Eleanor Roosevelt High School in Maryland, in their Science & Technology Program, and went on to graduate from the University of Virginia, School of Engineering and Applied Science, with a degree in Computer Science and an Engineering Business Minor.

My father lost everything. His business was destroyed, and immigrating to the United States was the only option left to him. I grew up largely without my parents — the war that emptied my country of people like my father was not the accident of history it's often taught as. Ronald Reagan told Americans he had stopped the spread of communism in El Salvador; in truth, his administration funded and armed the government waging that war, to protect an oligarchy long known as "the Fourteen Families" who controlled the country's wealth. Israel supplied the majority of El Salvador's military imports in the years leading into the war and trained the secret police that fed directly into the death squads. Separately, the U.S. Army's own School of the Americas, at Fort Benning, Georgia, trained the battalion responsible for some of the war's worst massacres. Reagan took office backed by the Heritage Foundation, campaigning on "Let's Make America Great Again" — a slogan history would recycle almost word for word decades later.

My father believed Reagan's version of events, and I was named after him.

That architecture didn't end with Reagan. The Heritage Foundation — the same organization that staffed and guided the Reagan administration in 1981 — still vets today's Republican Party, and still holds Reagan up as the baseline every Republican is measured against. Trump's own slogan, "Make America Great Again," is a direct descendant of Reagan's 1980 line. Today, Trump, his administration, and most Heritage-vetted Republicans accept money tied to Israel and rarely challenge it — the exceptions get punished. In May 2026, Rep. Thomas Massie, one of the only Republicans who refused AIPAC money and voted against foreign aid packages, lost his primary after pro-Israel PACs poured more than $15.5 million into the race against him, including $4.1 million from AIPAC's own super PAC, the United Democracy Project; total spending in that single House primary topped $32 million, a record. Rep. Marjorie Taylor Greene, who built her brand on "America First" and often noted she'd never taken AIPAC money, called Israel's war in Gaza a "genocide," broke publicly with Trump over it, and resigned from Congress effective January 5, 2026, a week after Trump denounced her as a "traitor." The pattern is the same one that funded El Salvador's death squads: loyalty to Israel is rewarded, and dissent is not survivable.

I've since reclaimed my name as my own. I wasn't named after Ronald Reagan — not the man, not what his administration did to my country, and not what it enabled. I try to live by character and principle. In that, I am his complete opposite. My name is mine.
